The Yanomami. An indigenous people of the Amazon rainforest numbering approximately thirty-five thousand who practice small-scale horticulture combined with hunting and gathering while maintaining fierce independence and cultural distinctiveness, though their territories face ongoing threats from illegal mining and disease. The Yanomami inhabit the Amazon rainforest along the Brazil-Venezuela border, particularly the Orinoco and Amazon river basins, across roughly nine point six million hectares of territory. They speak Yanomami languages, with distinct villages often speaking mutually intelligible but distinct dialects that are intimately tied to local identity and kinship systems. The Yanomami practice shifting cultivation, clearing small forest plots for yams, plantains, and other crops, then allowing the forest to regenerate. They combine agriculture with extensive hunting and gathering of rainforest resources. They organize into autonomous villages called shabonos, each containing roughly forty to one hundred fifty people, with minimal centralized authority. Decisions are made through consensus discussion, particularly among senior men. The Yanomami practice elaborate reciprocal exchange systems called daximi with other villages, trading goods, intermarrying, and creating alliances. These networks prevent excessive warfare and strengthen collective security. Their spiritual traditions center on shamanism, where shamans called xapiri communicate with forest spirits and perform healing and protective rituals central to community well-being. Since the nineteen eighties, the Yanomami face severe threats from illegal gold mining, which has introduced disease, contaminated water with mercury, and triggered violent conflicts. Malaria, measles, and other diseases have devastated populations.
